Algebra I · Lesson 7.1

The Cartesian Plane

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Chapter 7 is about pictures of equations, and drawing one takes a way to name a single point by numbers. Two number lines set at right angles are enough. One runs left and right, the other up and down, so every point has two counts, how far along and how far up. The first problem reads those counts off a walk, the second turns on their order.

Problem
The pair naming a point lists the count along first and the count up second, so a place 6 units along and 4 units up from where the two number lines cross is written (6,4)(6,4). A beetle starts at that crossing point, walks 11 units along, turns around and walks 3 units back the way it came, then walks 5 units up. Enter the first number of the pair naming where the beetle stops.
Show a hint
  • The first number of the pair is how far along the beetle ends up, not how far it walked in total. Work that count out from the moves along and leave the 5 units up out of it.
  • Walking 3 units back the way it came undoes part of the 11 units out, so the ending count along is smaller than 11.
Show the full solution
The beetle ends up 11−3=811−3=8 units along and 55 units up, so its pair is (8,5)(8,5) and the first number is 88​. Adding the two moves along instead of subtracting gives 1414, which is the total distance walked along and not the place the beetle stops.
Problem
Three points are (6,21)(6,21), (21,6)(21,6) and (13,27)(13,27). One of them sits furthest to the right. Enter the second number of that point's pair.
Show a hint
  • How far right a point sits comes from the first number of its pair, not the second. Compare the three first numbers before anything else.
  • The first numbers are 66, 2121 and 1313, so one point is clearly furthest right. Read off that point's second number.
Show the full solution
The first number of a pair is how far along, and those are 66, 2121 and 1313, so (21,6)(21,6) sits furthest to the right and its second number is 66​. Swapping the two roles would make (13,27)(13,27) look furthest right and give 2727, which is why the order inside a pair is fixed.
Key idea
An ordered pair names a point. Two number lines at right angles form the coordinate plane. The horizontal one is the xx-axis, the vertical one is the yy-axis, and they cross at the origin, (0,0)(0,0). The pair (a,b)(a,b) names the point reached by going aa along the xx-axis and bb up the yy-axis, so aa is its xx-coordinate and bb its yy-coordinate. Negative aa means left and negative bb means down. The pair is ordered, xx first and yy second, so (3,7)(3,7) and (7,3)(7,3) are different points.
Problem
A point sits 66 units to the left of the yy-axis and 33 units below the xx-axis. A second point sits 1010 units further left, at the same height. Enter the xx-coordinate of the second point.
Show a hint
  • Fix both coordinates of the first point before moving anything, and remember that left of the yy-axis puts its xx-coordinate below zero.
  • Moving further left subtracts, so the second xx-coordinate is 1010 less than the first. The height is the same for both points and is not needed here.
Show the full solution
The first point is 66 to the left, so x=−6x=−6, and 33 below, so y=−3y=−3. Moving 1010 further left subtracts 1010, giving −6−10=−16−6−10=−16​. Further left always means a smaller xx-coordinate. Adding the 1010 instead gives 44, which sits on the other side of the yy-axis entirely.
Problem
One of the points (0,−19)(0,−19) and (−19,0)(−19,0) lies on the xx-axis, and the other lies on the yy-axis. Enter the yy-coordinate of the one that lies on the yy-axis.
Show a hint
  • The origin (0,0)(0,0) lies on the yy-axis, and so does every point directly above or below it. Work out what those points all share in their first coordinate.
  • Both pairs contain a 00, so the position of that 00 is what decides. A first coordinate of 00 means x=0x=0, which is the yy-axis, and a second coordinate of 00 means y=0y=0, which is the xx-axis.
Show the full solution
Every point on the yy-axis has xx-coordinate 00, so (0,−19)(0,−19) is the one on the yy-axis, and its yy-coordinate is −19−19​. The common mistake is the reversal, since a coordinate of 00 puts a point on the axis named by the other letter. So x=0x=0 gives the yy-axis, y=0y=0 gives the xx-axis, and picking (−19,0)(−19,0) would have given 00.
Key idea
A point is on an axis exactly when one of its coordinates is zero. A point with x=0x=0 is no distance along from the origin, so it sits on the vertical axis, the yy-axis. A point with y=0y=0 is at no height, so it sits on the horizontal axis, the xx-axis. The coordinate set to zero is never the one the axis is named after. The origin has both coordinates zero and lies on both axes. The two axes cut the rest of the plane into four regions, each one a quadrant, and a point of either axis is on a boundary rather than inside a region, so it is in no quadrant.

Those four regions are the quadrants, numbered counterclockwise from the upper right, as in the figure. Which side of the yy-axis a point is on depends only on the sign of its xx-coordinate, and which side of the xx-axis only on the sign of its yy-coordinate. The next two problems need nothing beyond those two signs.

Problem
A point (m,n)(m,n) has m<0m<0 and n>0n>0, and nothing else about the two values is known. Enter the number of the quadrant the point lies in.
Show a hint
  • A negative xx-coordinate means the point is left of the yy-axis, and a positive yy-coordinate means it is above the xx-axis. Name that corner of the plane first.
  • Left and above is the upper left region. Count counterclockwise from the upper right to reach its number.
Show the full solution
Negative xx means left of the yy-axis and positive yy means above the xx-axis, so the point is in the upper left region, quadrant 22​. Neither value is needed, only the two signs. Every point with that sign pattern is in the same quadrant, however large or small mm and nn are.
Problem
The point (a,b)(a,b) lies in quadrant two, and nothing else about aa and bb is known. Enter the number of the quadrant that (b,a)(b,a) lies in.
Show a hint
  • Get the sign of aa and the sign of bb from quadrant two first, which is left of the yy-axis and above the xx-axis.
  • So aa is negative and bb is positive. In (b,a)(b,a) the positive number is the xx-coordinate and the negative one is the yy-coordinate.
Show the full solution
Quadrant two is left of the yy-axis and above the xx-axis, so a<0a<0 and b>0b>0. Then (b,a)(b,a) has a positive xx-coordinate and a negative yy-coordinate, which is right of the yy-axis and below the xx-axis, quadrant 44​. The quadrant depends on the signs alone, so no values for aa and bb are needed. In (a,b)(a,b) the negative number is first and in (b,a)(b,a) it is second, so the two points lie in different quadrants.
Key idea
The four quadrants. The axes cut the plane into four regions, numbered counterclockwise from the upper right. Quadrant one contains the points with x>0x>0 and y>0y>0, quadrant two those with x<0x<0 and y>0y>0, quadrant three those with x<0x<0 and y<0y<0, and quadrant four those with x>0x>0 and y<0y<0. Counterclockwise the sign pairs are (+,+)(+,+), (−,+)(−,+), (−,−)(−,−), (+,−)(+,−), one sign changing at each axis crossed. Nothing depends on the sizes, so (0.01,900)(0.01,900) and (5,5)(5,5) share a quadrant, and a point with a zero coordinate is on an axis and in no quadrant.

Any two points have a distance between them, and when they share a coordinate that distance is already a length on a single number line. Two points at the same height differ only in how far along they sit, so the gap between them is the difference of their xx-coordinates. A distance is never negative, so subtract the smaller from the larger.

Problem
The points (−12,5)(−12,5) and (21,5)(21,5) have the same yy-coordinate, so the segment joining them is horizontal. Enter its length.
Show a hint
  • Only the xx-values differ, so the length is the distance from −12−12 to 2121 on the number line. Counting across 00 is a safe way to do it.
  • The length is 21−(−12)21−(−12). Subtracting a negative adds, so the result is larger than 2121, not smaller.
Show the full solution
Both endpoints have y=5y=5, so the length is the difference of the xx-coordinates, 21−(−12)=21+12=3321−(−12)=21+12=33​. Computing 21−12=921−12=9 instead is what comes of dropping the sign on −12−12. One endpoint is 1212 units left of the yy-axis and the other 2121 units right, so those two distances add.
Fun fact
Pierre de Fermat worked out coordinate geometry on his own, slightly earlier than the version the plane is named for. His manuscript circulated in 1636 but was not printed until after his death, so the idea arrived twice.
Problem
The points A=(2,−1)A=(2,−1) and B=(14,4)B=(14,4) have no coordinate in common, so a single subtraction will not give the distance. The point C=(14,−1)C=(14,−1) lies directly to the right of AA and directly below BB, so triangle ABCABC has a right angle at CC, one leg horizontal and one leg vertical. Find the two leg lengths, then use the Pythagorean theorem. Enter the distance from AA to BB.
Show a hint
  • A horizontal segment has length equal to the difference of the two xx-coordinates, and a vertical segment the difference of the two yy-coordinates. Take each difference in the order that makes it positive, and watch the subtraction of −1−1.
  • The legs come out 1212 and 55. The theorem gives the square of ABAB as the sum of the squares of those two.
Show the full solution
The horizontal leg is 14−2=1214−2=12 and the vertical leg is 4−(−1)=54−(−1)=5, so AB2=122+52=144+25=169AB2=122+52=144+25=169 and AB=169=13AB=169​=13​. One leg is horizontal and the other vertical, so the angle between them is right and the theorem applies. Adding the legs gives 1717, the length of the path through CC rather than the direct distance.
Key idea
The distance formula. For points (x1,y1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x2​,y2​), the point (x2,y1)(x2​,y1​) is the right-angle corner of a triangle with a horizontal leg of length ∣x2−x1∣∣x2​−x1​∣ and a vertical leg of length ∣y2−y1∣∣y2​−y1​∣, and the angle there is right because the axes meet at right angles. The Pythagorean theorem then gives d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2.d=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2​. Each difference is squared, so its sign has no effect and subtracting in either order gives the same distance. When the two points share a coordinate, one difference is 00 and what is left is the single subtraction from before.

The point halfway along the segment joining two points is their midpoint. On a single number line, halfway between two numbers is their average. How far along a point sits and how high it sits are each measured on a number line of their own, so averaging the two coordinates separately is worth a try, and the next two problems check it.

Problem
A segment has endpoints (−6,−5)(−6,−5) and (10,19)(10,19). Enter the yy-coordinate of the midpoint of that segment.
Show a hint
  • The midpoint has two coordinates and only one of them is wanted here. The −6−6 and the 1010 give the xx-coordinate of the midpoint, and the yy-coordinate comes from the other two numbers.
  • The yy-coordinate of the midpoint is the average of −5−5 and 1919. Add the two heights first, keeping the sign on −5−5, then halve the total.
Show the full solution
The yy-coordinate of the midpoint is the average of the two endpoint heights, −5+192=142=72−5+19​=214​=7​. Counting from the lower end gives the same value, since 19−(−5)=2419−(−5)=24 and half of that added to −5−5 is −5+12=7−5+12=7.
Problem
The midpoint of the segment joining A=(−3,9)A=(−3,9) and BB is M=(5,−4)M=(5,−4). Enter the yy-coordinate of BB.
Show a hint
  • The midpoint's yy-coordinate is the average of the two endpoints' yy-coordinates. Here that average is known and one of the two numbers being averaged is not.
  • Call the yy-coordinate of BB simply yy and write 9+y2=−429+y​=−4, then multiply both sides by 22 to clear the fraction and solve.
Show the full solution
Write B=(x,y)B=(x,y). The midpoint's yy-coordinate is the average of the two endpoints', so 9+y2=−429+y​=−4, giving 9+y=−89+y=−8 and y=−17y=−17​. As a check, the drop from 99 to −4−4 is 1313, and another 1313 below −4−4 is −17−17. Averaging the two given heights gives 9+(−4)2=5229+(−4)​=25​, the height halfway from AA to MM rather than the height of BB.
Key idea
The midpoint is the average of the coordinates. The midpoint of the segment joining (x1,y1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x2​,y2​) is M=(x1+x22, y1+y22).M=(2x1​+x2​​, 2y1​+y2​​). Going from one endpoint to the other changes the xx-coordinate by x2−x1x2​−x1​, so half of that change from x1x1​ is x1+x2−x12=x1+x22x1​+2x2​−x1​​=2x1​+x2​​, with the same work for the height. Multiplying by 22 gives x1+x2=2xMx1​+x2​=2xM​, where xMxM​ is the midpoint's own xx-coordinate. When one endpoint and the midpoint are known, that leaves the missing coordinate as the only unknown.

Everything in this lesson comes from the two coordinates of a point. Naming a quadrant takes only their signs, a distance between two points takes the two differences, and a midpoint takes the two averages. The last two problems use more than one of the three at once.

Problem
A segment runs from A=(−7,−2)A=(−7,−2) to B=(5,14)B=(5,14), and MM is the midpoint of that segment. Enter the distance from AA to MM.
Show a hint
  • The midpoint is halfway along, so its distance from an endpoint is half the whole length. Finding the whole length first avoids computing the midpoint at all.
  • The two differences from AA to BB are 1212 and 1616. Put those through the distance formula, then halve.
Show the full solution
The differences are 5−(−7)=125−(−7)=12 and 14−(−2)=1614−(−2)=16, so the whole length is 122+162=400=20122+162​=400​=20, and half of it is 1010​. The other route agrees, since the midpoint is (−1,6)(−1,6) and 62+82=100=1062+82​=100​=10. Each difference from AA to MM is half the matching difference from AA to BB, so halving the whole length gives the same value.
Problem
The midpoint of the segment joining A=(−3,7)A=(−3,7) and BB lies on the xx-axis, and the xx-coordinate of BB is 4545. Enter the distance from AA to BB.
Show a hint
  • Only the second coordinate of BB is unknown, so write B=(45,k)B=(45,k). A point of the xx-axis has yy-coordinate 00, so the midpoint's second coordinate is known even though the midpoint is not. That is one equation for kk.
  • The two second coordinates average to 00, so 7+k2=027+k​=0. Once BB is known, the two differences are 4848 and −14−14.
Show the full solution
Write B=(45,k)B=(45,k). A point of the xx-axis has yy-coordinate 00, so 7+k2=027+k​=0, giving k=−7k=−7 and B=(45,−7)B=(45,−7). The differences are 45−(−3)=4845−(−3)=48 and −7−7=−14−7−7=−14, so the distance is 482+(−14)2=2304+196=2500=50482+(−14)2​=2304+196​=2500​=50​. Setting x=0x=0 instead puts the zero on the wrong coordinate, and the xx-coordinate of BB is already given.

The plane is built. Every ordered pair names one point, every point has exactly one pair, and both the distance formula and the midpoint formula come out of that naming alone. Lesson 7.2, Graphing Linear Equations, is about the pairs that make an equation true.

Practice these ideas

Practice
A point lies 2424 units to the left of the yy-axis and 66 units above the xx-axis. Enter its xx-coordinate.
Show the solution
The horizontal position is the xx-coordinate, and 2424 units left of the yy-axis is 2424 units in the negative direction, so the xx-coordinate is −24−24​. The 66 units above the xx-axis is the vertical position, so the point is (−24,6)(−24,6).
Practice
The points (20,−11)(20,−11) and (−11,20)(−11,20) are built from the same two numbers in opposite orders. Exactly one of them sits above the xx-axis. Enter the xx-coordinate of that point.
Show the solution
The second numbers are −11−11 and 2020, so (−11,20)(−11,20) is the point above the xx-axis, and its xx-coordinate is −11−11​. Answering 2020 means reading the pair in the wrong order, since 2020 is that point's yy-coordinate.
Practice
A point lies on the yy-axis, 2626 units above the origin. Enter its xx-coordinate.
Show the solution
A point on the yy-axis sits directly above or below the origin with no horizontal step, so its xx-coordinate is 00​. The 2626 is the vertical distance, so the point is (0,26)(0,26). The common slip is to read yy-axis as y=0y=0, but the coordinate that is 00 there is xx.
Practice
Seven points are (−9,2)(−9,2), (0,7)(0,7), (3,−4)(3,−4), (−1,−1)(−1,−1), (8,0)(8,0), (−5,−6)(−5,−6) and (2,9)(2,9). Enter how many of them lie inside a quadrant rather than on an axis.
Show the solution
Of the seven, (0,7)(0,7) and (8,0)(8,0) have a zero coordinate and so are on an axis, which leaves 55​. A point is on an axis whenever either of its coordinates is zero, and no point on an axis is inside a quadrant.
Practice
Enter the number of the quadrant containing the point (−2.5,−40)(−2.5,−40).
Show the solution
The first coordinate is negative, so the point is left of the yy-axis, and the second is negative, so the point is below the xx-axis. That is the lower left region, quadrant 33​. The sizes 2.52.5 and 4040 make no difference, since a quadrant depends only on the two signs.
Practice
The product of a point's two coordinates is positive, and its xx-coordinate is positive. Enter the number of the quadrant the point lies in.
Show the solution
A positive product means the two coordinates share a sign, and the xx-coordinate is positive, so the yy-coordinate is positive as well. Right of the yy-axis and above the xx-axis is quadrant 11​. Without the fact about xx, both coordinates could be negative instead, which is quadrant three.
Practice
The point (c+5, c+12)(c+5, c+12) lies on the xx-axis. Enter cc.
Show the solution
A point on the xx-axis has yy-coordinate 00, so c+12=0c+12=0 and c=−12c=−12​. The point is then (−7,0)(−7,0). Setting the first entry to zero instead gives c=−5c=−5, which puts the point on the yy-axis rather than the xx-axis.
Practice
Enter the distance between (−8,−6)(−8,−6) and (15,−6)(15,−6).
Show the solution
Both points have y=−6y=−6, so the segment is horizontal and the distance is 15−(−8)=15+8=2315−(−8)=15+8=23​. When two points share a coordinate, only the other pair of coordinates matters, and the distance is the larger minus the smaller.
Practice
Enter the distance between (7,−21)(7,−21) and (7,9)(7,9).
Show the solution
Both points have x=7x=7, so the distance is 9−(−21)=9+21=309−(−21)=9+21=30​. A shared xx-coordinate means a vertical segment, and a shared yy-coordinate means a horizontal one.
Practice
Enter the distance between (2,−3)(2,−3) and (26,4)(26,4).
Show the solution
The differences are 26−2=2426−2=24 and 4−(−3)=74−(−3)=7, so the distance is 242+72=576+49=625=25242+72​=576+49​=625​=25​. Reading 4−(−3)4−(−3) as 11 is the usual slip, and it gives 577577​ instead.
Practice
Enter the distance from the origin to the point (−9,−40)(−9,−40).
Show the solution
Taking (x1,y1)=(0,0)(x1​,y1​)=(0,0), the differences are −9−9 and −40−40, so the distance is (−9)2+(−40)2=81+1600=1681=41(−9)2+(−40)2​=81+1600​=1681​=41​. With the origin as the first point, x1x1​ and y1y1​ are both zero, so the legs of the right triangle have lengths 99 and 4040, the sizes of the point's own coordinates.
Practice
The distance between (−5,3)(−5,3) and (4,21)(4,21) simplifies to a5a5​, where aa is a whole number. Enter aa.
Show the solution
The differences are 4−(−5)=94−(−5)=9 and 21−3=1821−3=18, so the distance is 92+182=81+324=40592+182​=81+324​=405​. Since 405=81⋅5405=81⋅5, that is 815=9581​5​=95​, so a=9a=9​. Splitting 405405 as 9⋅459⋅45 gives 345345​, the same number in a form that is not simplified, so take the largest perfect square factor, 8181.
Practice
Enter the xx-coordinate of the midpoint of the segment joining (−13,−20)(−13,−20) and (49,6)(49,6).
Show the solution
The xx-coordinates average to −13+492=362=182−13+49​=236​=18​. Each coordinate of the midpoint is averaged on its own, so the −20−20 and the 66 are used only for the midpoint's yy-coordinate, which is −7−7.
Practice
Enter the yy-coordinate of the midpoint of the segment joining (6,−3)(6,−3) and (20,10)(20,10).
Show the solution
The yy-coordinates average to −3+102=722−3+10​=27​​. With whole-number coordinates, the average is a whole number only when the two are both even or both odd, so a fraction here is correct rather than a sign of a slip.
Practice
The segment with endpoints P=(−7,3)P=(−7,3) and QQ has midpoint (4,−6)(4,−6). Enter the xx-coordinate of QQ.
Show the solution
Writing Q=(q,r)Q=(q,r), the xx-coordinates average to 44, so −7+q2=42−7+q​=4, giving −7+q=8−7+q=8 and q=15q=15​. As a check, −7−7 to 44 is a step of 1111, and 4+11=154+11=15.
Practice
The midpoint of the segment joining (−31,4)(−31,4) and (t,10)(t,10) lies on the yy-axis. Enter tt.
Show the solution
A point on the yy-axis has xx-coordinate 00, so −31+t2=02−31+t​=0, giving −31+t=0−31+t=0 and t=31t=31​. The yy-axis is the line x=0x=0, not y=0y=0, so only the first coordinates matter here. Averaging 44 and 1010 instead gives 77 for every tt, so that reading has no solution.
Practice
A segment has one endpoint at (−6,1)(−6,1) and its midpoint at (14,22)(14,22). Enter the length of the whole segment.
Show the solution
The differences from (−6,1)(−6,1) to (14,22)(14,22) are 2020 and 2121, so half the segment is 202+212=400+441=841=29202+212​=400+441​=841​=29 and the whole segment is 5858​. Working the long way gives the same number. The other endpoint is (34,43)(34,43), and 402+422=3364=58402+422​=3364​=58.
